newsitem.title: UK: Mark nudges higher in Europe in thin volumes.
newsitem.headline: Mark nudges higher in Europe in thin volumes.

text.p: The mark was slightly firmer on its European cross rates early on Tuesday after U.S. asset market turbulence overnight prompted additional demand for marks amid a temporary pullback in dollar/mark.

U.S. stocks and bonds fell sharply overnight after Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said Japan may sell some of its U.S. Treasury bond holdings for gold as a way of stabilising exchange rates. He later said the comments were misinterpreted.
Trading conditions on European crosses were very quiet and ranges were small, however, as the summer holiday season began to cramp volumes, traders said.

"The markets overreacted to the Japanese comments overnight and don't think we're likely to see any active Japanese disinvestment from Treasuries," said Nick Parsons, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas.
However, Parsons said it is possible that the flow of Japanese funds into Treasuries may ebb for a period and this may act as a longer term drag on the bond market and dollar.

More generalised global bond market worries as a result could have knock on effects in the more peripheral European markets like Italy, for example, and undermine some of the lira's recent bond-driven gains, he said.
The yen was the main net mover on Hashimoto's comments, however, and dollar/mark retrieved all its overnight losses in early trade and was higher than Monday's close in Europe
At 0858 GMT, mark/lira was trading at 978.30/80 compared with 977.70/978.00 late Monday.
BTP's stayed relatively buoyant and the 10-year yield spread over German bunds hovered near record lows at 118 basis points.

The remainder of Italian cities inflation data for June was published late Monday and confirmed expectations of a drop in the national inflation rate to between 1.4 and 1.5 percent from 1.6 percent in May.
Traders said there were also some concerns about the sustainability of the lira's recent gains to four-month highs.

"The Japanese story was probably a storm in a tea cup but there are some worries about the lira being this far above its central ERM rate if you believe it will be in the first wave of EMU," said Peter Wood, currency trader at the Bank of Boston.
There is growing official support for using existing central rates in the European exchange rate mechanism as the fixing rates for European monetrary union in 1999.
The lira's midrate is 990 per mark but some analysts say its current spot rate is not necessarily inconsistent with this.

If ERM mid-rates are used and Italy qualifies for EMU, then the mark/lira forward rate for January 1 1999 must be 990. But because of the existing Italy/German interest rate differential a forward rate at 990 in January 1999 would imply a spot rate now in the region of 960 - two percent stronger than at present.
Moreover, mark/lira implied volatility levels remain near historic lows at just 4.00/4.35 percent on a one-year horizon.

Elsewhere, the latest official comments out of Europe continued to be positive on European monetary union. Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said it was important EMU starts on time and a delay would risk German job losses.
Mark/French franc was trading at 3.3755/58 compared with 3.3729/34 late Monday.

Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said later he was confident all EU countries, including France, would take all necessary steps to complete EMU on time and that these efforts would ensure the euro was as credible as the mark and franc.

The mark was given some support in early trade from a bigger-than-expected 0.5 percent rise in May but analysts said there was still no sign yet of these prices filtering through to final consumer prices.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
